The Delian Construction

ParadoxesAlgebra
Game: A reader says a clever drawing doubles a cube with only a ruler and a compass; your job is to find out whether it really works.
How to play: Change N, the number of radials. The drawing shows where the construction puts its points on the vertical line AB, and the table says how far each is from where the reader claims it should be.

Filled dots on AB: what the construction gives. Rings beside them: where the claim says they should be.

Distances from A along AB (AD = 1, AB = 2). The last column is the construction minus the claim, times 1000.
kConstruction2k/NGap × 1000
Look for the math

Doubling the cube means building a cube with twice the volume of a given one, so a side ∛2 times as long. The Greeks tried with ruler and compass; it cannot be done, and this drawing, which claims to do it, is a good place to see how an impossibility hides.

What the reader claims

Draw a right triangle with AB = 2 and BC = 1, find the point x on AB with Ax = √2 (a compass arc from A of radius AE, where AD = DE = 1 so that AE = √2), then draw the lines that make the “Golden Triangle” BFD. Divide BC into N equal parts, join each division to A, and carry the points where the radials cross DF and BF down to AB with parallels. The claim is that on AB they mark 1, 21/N, 22/N, …, 2, a geometric progression, and for N = 3 the second point would be ∛2.

What the drawing really does

The construction is built from straight lines, so it can only send the equally spaced points on BC to positions on AB by a projective (Möbius) map, never an exponential. The logic test found that the point for division k is exactly at distance (1 + (√2 − 1)t) / (1 − (1 − √2/2)t) from A with t = k/N, by two independent ways of computing it, for every N from 2 to 20. That function and 2t agree at t = 0, ½ and 1 (so the ends and the middle are exactly right, and the middle point is truly √2 for even N), and differ by at most 0.0024, about 0.13%, in between. For N = 3 the “cube root of 2” point is at 1.26120 instead of 1.25992, and its cube is 2.006, not 2. The mistake is hard to see exactly because the drawing is so close.

Why it cannot work

A length built with ruler and compass lies in a chain of square-root extensions of the rationals, so the degree of the number over the rationals is a power of 2. But ∛2 is a root of x³ − 2, which has no rational root (a rational root would be ±1 or ±2, and none works), so it is irreducible of degree 3. Not a power of 2, so the cube cannot be doubled by these tools (Wantzel, 1837).

Set N = 12, the reader’s case, and look at the bars: where is the error largest? Then set N = 2, the one case where the construction gives exactly what it claims.
